Here’s a draft for that next section, in the same voice as the Chert / PyMuPDF bits:

---

# Insurance Requirement Matching

Once documents are in the patient record, Unburden evaluates them against a structured insurance policy — not a free-form LLM prompt. Each requirement is encoded with retrieval terms, acceptable document types, temporal windows, numeric thresholds, and phrase-level accept/reject rules.

**Retrieval** finds candidate passages per page by matching those terms, so every citation stays tied to a real source quote.

**Verification** then decides whether a candidate actually satisfies the requirement: the quote must appear verbatim in the extracted page text, the document type must be allowed, and date/numeric constraints must hold. Ambiguous or disqualifying language is flagged for review rather than auto-accepted.

For semantic judgment beyond keyword lists, we layer in **DeBERTa NLI** (entailment / neutral / contradiction). Strong contradiction can reject a passage; strong entailment is only a support signal — structured checks still decide acceptance. Candidates land as **support**, **insufficient**, or **contradiction**; a requirement is **READY** only when there is at least one support citation and zero contradictions — otherwise **NEEDS_REVIEW**.

---

# Insurance Requirement Matching with DeBERTa

To figure out whether a passage actually supports an insurance requirement, we use a DeBERTa-v3 NLI model. It takes the extracted passage and the requirement as a premise–hypothesis pair and scores entailment, neutral, or contradiction. We calibrated the decision thresholds on TREC clinical-trials data instead of fine-tuning weights, and structured checks (dates, numbers, document types, quote-in-source) still decide what gets accepted — the model is there for the semantic support / contradiction call that keyword matching alone misses.

content.text:
## Challenges we ran into

**Getting Chert + LiveKit stable.** Outbound FaceTime took a while — wrong/missing config, calls that never rang, then a call that connected but hung up without talking. Later we hit stale agent workers that timed out waiting for an unmuted audio track, and the greeting kept getting cut off because capture started too early.

**FaceTime photos broke text extraction.** Normal PDFs parsed fine with PyMuPDF. FaceTime captures were basically images, so we had to fall back to Tesseract OCR. That got text out, but with enough typos that the same lab report went from ~96% match on a clean upload to ~50% over FaceTime — so we added deterministic post-OCR cleanup instead of throwing an LLM at it.

**Figuring out the matching model.** Keyword/rule matching alone wasn’t enough, and it wasn’t obvious whether we needed a medical-specific model. We looked at PubMedBERT + MedNLI, but it wasn’t clearly better here. What worked was keeping Milestone 3’s structured checks (dates, numbers, doc types, quote-in-source) and using DeBERTa only as a support/contradiction signal. There’s also basically no public dataset of real PA requirements paired with labeled clinical evidence, so we used TREC for threshold calibration rather than trying to fine-tune our way out of it.

**Making statuses make sense in the UI.** We had accept / needs review / not established floating around differently across TREC, NLI, citations, and requirements. Standardizing on support / insufficient / contradiction, wiring clinician overrides, and simplifying rollups to READY vs NEEDS_REVIEW took a few rounds — plus fixing things like citations disappearing, long reloads on status change, and delete/upload briefly desyncing the insurance view.
